body.text: In brief
• Pugh completed about 15km of swimming over three days, wearing only trunks, goggles and a swimming cap.
• The endurance swimmer has previously crossed the North Pole and swum the entire Hudson River.
United Kingdom endurance swimmer Lewis Pugh has swum in the North Pole and Antarctica to draw attention to environmental causes.
But battling freezing waters and extreme conditions hasn't prepared him for his latest challenge: swimming the Strait of Hormuz while tankers are attacked and blown up nearby.
Pugh, who is a United Nations Patron of the Oceans, spent three days this week swimming parts of the dangerous waterway to highlight how the war with Iran threatens the area's habitat and wildlife.

Wearing only swimming trunks, goggles and a cap bearing the UN logo, the athlete started from the Musandam peninsula, on the southern tip of the strait, and ended by rounding the Cape of Hormuz, completing about 15km in total.
Pugh is believed to be the first person to undertake a long-distance swim there since the war started.
The swimmer said that minutes after he entered the water on Monday, he heard two loud explosions that rocked the sea.
"I looked up and I could see that an oil tanker about 4km away had been hit,” he told The Associated Press after he returned to London.
"The explosion was so loud, two booms, and then fighter jets coming in. And at that moment I realised we have to get out of here right now."
Pugh, 56, managed to complete his feat after more stops and starts, including passing another vessel that, after being attacked, sent fireballs into the sky.
"Most people, when they think about the Strait of Hormuz, they think of a shipping lane," he said.
"But it is also one of the most beautiful places I have ever been … it's one of the treasure troves of the natural world."
"With all these ships being sunk, this area is under severe threat," he added.
"It’s going to take years, decades for this area to recover."
Oil pollution threatens wildlife

Iran has in recent weeks increased attacks on vessels that it claimed travelled along unauthorised routes in the strait as it seeks to impose its control on the crucial waterway, where a fifth of all oil traded passed through before the US and Israel launched the war on 28 February.
Several tankers have also struck sea mines laid by Iran, in some cases exploding and bursting into flames, among them one that was carrying over two million barrels of oil last month.
Pugh warned of how oil leaking from the dozens of tankers damaged since February could create lasting problems for the region's animals, as well as its coastlines, coral reefs and mangrove forests.

He described seeing large numbers of dolphins following his boat as he sailed in, as well as turtles and ospreys. He also marvelled at the hundreds of turtles he saw while swimming along the Omani coast before the war.
“When oil gets in there, when chemical pollution gets in there, it becomes very, very difficult to clean up that type of mess," he said.
"It lasts for generations."
Swim challenge takes place as vessels were attacked
Pugh has had plenty of experience facing extreme temperatures and predators, including great white sharks. But swimming in a conflict zone presented entirely new dangers.

To stay safe, the challenge was done in sections over three days, with a total of about six and a half hours of swimming. The athlete recalled seeing a gas carrier being struck while he was returning to the harbour on the second day.

"I’ll never ever forget going past that gas carrier, the smell of the chemicals and then the flames; they were literally like fireballs going up into the sky. Around the ship, the water was on fire," Pugh said.
"And to think of the impact which a casualty like this has on nature — it was very, very acute."
Using sport to lobby for green causes

Pugh has spent much of the past 40 years swimming in places from Antarctica to the Red Sea and from the English Channel to urge more action to protect marine environments from climate change, pollution and biodiversity loss.

He was the first athlete to swim across the North Pole and complete a long-distance swim in every one of the world’s oceans. In 2023, he swam all 507km of the Hudson River to highlight the importance of clean rivers.
His foundation says the challenges have helped secure official agreements to protect more than 3.5 million square km of vulnerable ocean.
Some have dubbed Pugh’s blend of epic swimming and political outreach as "Speedo diplomacy".
"Sport opens doors, it creates dialogue, it enables people to start thinking about these important issues," Pugh said.
"My message is very simple," he added.
"We’ve got to stop the war. We’ve got to open the strait, and we’ve got to clean up the pollution."
